title: Parashurama's challenge
hook: the wedding party is riding home when the sky goes dark and a man with an axe steps onto the road

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four weddings. Four brothers, four brides, and the whole city of Mithila celebrating. Did you share in someone else's small joy? Today the wedding party heads home, and the road turns strange. Day five hundred twelve.

It should be the happiest caravan in the story. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers, and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly. At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, which is a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha, the family priest, reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. Then a wind rises. The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.
screen: `THE HAPPIEST CARAVAN IN THE STORY.` → `BAD BIRDS, GOOD DEER.` → `A MAN WITH AN AXE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, an arrow in the other, the axe across his shoulder. He is the son of the sage Jamadagni, from the family of Bhrigu. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe, and counts him among the avatars of Vishnu. He is a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons. After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Now he has heard that a young prince named Rama has broken Shiva's great bow at Janaka's court. So he has brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two great bows. One went to Shiva, the other to Vishnu. The gods wanted to know which of the two was stronger, and a contest broke out. In his telling, one great roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack, and the gods of the story judged Vishnu the stronger. Shiva's bow passed down to the kings of Videha. That is the one Rama broke. Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's own family, and here it is. String this one, he tells Rama, fit an arrow to it, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs him. You're a brahmin, he says. You laid down your weapons. You gave the earth away. Spare my son. Parashurama doesn't even answer the king. He speaks only to Rama. And here is the strange heart of today: one Rama is facing another. In later tradition, both are Vishnu come down to earth.
screen: `A FIRE NO ONE CAN LOOK AT.` · `THE SON OF JAMADAGNI.` · `TWO BOWS: SHIVA'S AND VISHNU'S.` · `STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.` · then, large: `ONE RAMA FACES ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think of a challenge that came at you lately, from someone older, louder, or very sure of themselves. Don't answer it yet. Just notice what happens in the body: the jaw, the shoulders, the belly. On each breath out, let one of those places soften a little. You're not giving in. You're making room to answer well. The bell holds the time.
Parashurama's challenge. The axe-bearing son of Jamadagni meets Rama on the road home and holds out Vishnu's bow: string it, and then we fight.
Your line: Parashurama's challenge. Today, when someone tests you, take one full breath before you pick up the bow. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Parashurama as one of Vishnu's ten avatars, usually listed sixth, and mark his birth on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. a terrifying sage blocks the road and challenges your newly married son. what do you do?
options: plead with him to spare the boy.
fork.reveal: the king begs him, reminding him he laid down his weapons. Parashurama ignores him and turns to Rama.

original.note: Sanskrit paraśurāma: Rama with the paraśu, the axe. Valmiki mostly calls him Jamadagnya, son of Jamadagni.

trapdoor: what you thought: Parashurama is just an angry sage.
what it means: he's a brahmin warrior carrying Vishnu's bow, come to test the prince who broke Shiva's.
what a scholar hears: in the later lists of ten avatars he's usually sixth and Rama seventh, so this road meeting reads as one avatar meeting the next.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 74–75 (omens on the road; Parashurama appears; the two bows)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; the Baroda critical edition differs. Please confirm.
Valmiki mostly names him Jamadagnya or Bhargava Rama; the name Parashurama is used here as the index does. Confirm framing as 'later tradition calls him'.
The contest of the two bows: the script says Vishnu's roar (humkara) made Shiva's bow slack. Confirm detail.
Avatar lists vary; 'usually sixth' is softened deliberately.
The story of his war on the kshatriyas is given only in outline (no count of twenty-one times).
Reviewer: 'a king killed his father' softened to 'killed in a feud with a royal house'; traditions differ on whether Kartavirya Arjuna or his sons killed Jamadagni. Confirm.

Reviewer: the bow contest ranks Vishnu over Shiva. It is in Valmiki (Bala 75), but Shaiva listeners may hear it as sectarian; the script now frames it as Parashurama's telling. A Keeper should confirm the framing is fair to Shaiva traditions.
